title: Marxist and Dependency Approaches

cards.h: The view from the bottom of the system
cards.b:
Realists see states competing for power. Liberals see states cooperating. Marxists ask a different question: who gains from the international system, and who pays?

For Marxist and dependency thinkers, world politics is shaped by capitalism and class. The rich "core" grows rich by drawing wealth from the poor "periphery". Rivalry between states is a side effect of competition between capitalists.

This approach matters for the exam because it explains imperialism, underdevelopment, the Global South's demands (NIEO, UNCTAD) and India's own colonial experience. It is also the best theory to cite when asked about inequality in globalisation.

Expect questions on Lenin, Wallerstein's world-system, dependency theory (Frank, Prebisch, Amin), and neo-Gramscian ideas (Cox). A critique card at the end shows you can weigh the theory.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels (The Communist Manifesto, 1848) argued that history moves through class struggle. Capitalism spreads across the globe to find markets, cheap labour and raw materials: "it creates a world after its own image".

Marx did not write a full theory of international relations. Later Marxists did. Their shared ideas:

  • Economics comes first. The base (the mode of production) shapes politics, the state and war.
  • The state is a tool of the ruling class (or at least tied to it).
  • The unit of analysis is class and the world capitalist system, not the nation-state.
  • Capitalism produces inequality between and within countries.
  • Real change needs a change in the system. Reform within it is limited.

J.A. Hobson, a British liberal economist, wrote Imperialism: A Study (1902). He said imperialism arose from underconsumption at home. Rich investors needed outlets abroad.

V.I. Lenin took this up in Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916). It is the central Marxist text on IR.

Lenin's argument

  • Competitive capitalism turns into monopoly capitalism. Banks and industry merge into finance capital.
  • Rich countries have surplus capital. They export capital to colonies, where profits are higher.
  • Cartels and great powers divide the world. Capitalism develops unevenly, so rivals demand a redivision.
  • So WWI was an inter-imperialist war. Imperialism also gives the working class of the core a share ("labour aristocracy"), which delays revolution.

Others: Rosa Luxemburg (The Accumulation of Capital, 1913), Nikolai Bukharin (Imperialism and World Economy, 1915). Karl Kautsky disagreed and predicted "ultra-imperialism": a peaceful joint rule by the great powers.

After 1945, Latin American thinkers asked why the poor stayed poor. Raul Prebisch, head of the UN Economic Commission for Latin America (ECLA) and later first Secretary-General of UNCTAD (1964), and Hans Singer argued in 1949-50 that the terms of trade turn against primary exporters. Prices of raw materials fall relative to manufactures. Their remedy was import-substitution industrialisation.

Andre Gunder Frank

In "The Development of Underdevelopment" (1966) and Capitalism and Underdevelopment in Latin America (1967), Frank said poverty is not a stage before development. It is created by integration into the world market. He described a chain of metropolis and satellite, where surplus flows upward. His remedy: break links with the core.

Samir Amin

An Egyptian economist. Unequal Development (1973) described a periphery with a distorted economy, built to serve the core. He called for "delinking".

Paul Baran (The Political Economy of Growth, 1957) and Walter Rodney (How Europe Underdeveloped Africa, 1972) share this line.

Not all dependency thinkers wanted a full break from the world market.

Fernando Henrique Cardoso and Enzo Faletto, Dependency and Development in Latin America (written 1967-69; English edition 1979), argued that dependency does not rule out growth. They described associated-dependent development: local elites, multinationals and the state build industry together, but on terms set by the core. Cardoso later served as President of Brazil (1995-2002).

Johan Galtung, "A Structural Theory of Imperialism" (1971), said the world is a set of centres and peripheries, and each country has its own centre (the elite) and periphery. Imperialism rests on a harmony of interest between the elite in the centre and the elite in the periphery, and on a disharmony between the masses.

This is why dependency is called structural: it is a relationship, not just a policy.

Immanuel Wallerstein, The Modern World-System (vol. 1, 1974), argues that since the "long sixteenth century" there has been one capitalist world-economy. It has a single division of labour, many states and no world empire.

  • Core: strong states, advanced industry, high wages. Gets the surplus.
  • Periphery: weak states, raw materials, low-wage labour.
  • Semi-periphery: in between. It gets exploited by the core and exploits the periphery. It keeps the system stable.

Countries can move between zones, but the system as a whole keeps the structure. Hegemons (Dutch, British, American) rise and fall in long cycles. Wallerstein said the system would eventually reach a crisis.

Antonio Gramsci (Prison Notebooks, 1929-35) stressed hegemony: ruling classes keep power through consent, culture and ideas, not only force.

Robert Cox, "Social Forces, States and World Orders" (1981), used this in IR. His famous line: "Theory is always for someone and for some purpose". He split theory into problem-solving (accepts the order, as realism does) and critical (asks how the order came about and how it can change).

Cox's three forces

Material capabilities, ideas, and institutions. They combine into a historic bloc. A world order becomes hegemonic when its ideas are widely accepted, as US-led liberalism after 1945 was. International organisations help spread them.

Others in this line: Stephen Gill, on the "new constitutionalism" of free-market rules, and the Frankfurt School thinkers Adorno, Horkheimer and Habermas. In IR, Andrew Linklater (Men and Citizens, 1982) took critical theory to questions of community and emancipation.

What it explains well

  • Imperialism, colonial extraction and unequal trade.
  • Why many poor states stay stuck in raw-material exports.
  • Debt, structural adjustment, and the demand for NIEO.
  • The link between economic power and political power.

What it struggles with

  • East Asian success. South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore grew rich within the world market. China too, after 1978.
  • It is economically reductionist: it ignores security, culture, identity and domestic politics.
  • It underrates the role of local elites and bad governance.
  • Robert Brenner (1977) attacked Wallerstein for putting trade ahead of production relations.
  • Bill Warren (1980) argued capitalism actually develops the periphery.
  • The Soviet bloc, supposedly anti-capitalist, also built empires.

A balanced answer: the approach is strong on structure but weak on agency.

cards.h: Drain theory, NIEO and the Global South
cards.b:
India's own thinkers had a dependency-like view long before Frank.

  • Dadabhai Naoroji's Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) set out the drain of wealth: Britain took resources out of India without return.
  • R.C. Dutt's The Economic History of India (1901-03) documented de-industrialisation.

After independence, Nehru built a state-led, import-substituting economy, close to Prebisch's advice. India helped found UNCTAD (1964) and the G-77 (1964), and pushed the NIEO (1974).

Today, India speaks as a voice of the Global South. During its G20 presidency (2023) it held the "Voice of Global South Summit", and the African Union joined the G20. It argues for debt relief, climate finance and fair trade rules at the WTO.

But India is no longer a pure periphery. Its software exports, new economy and middle-income status mean a mix of core-like and periphery-like traits, which fits Wallerstein's "semi-periphery". Critics also note India's own domestic inequality.

"Critically examine the Marxist approach to international relations."
"Explain Lenin's theory of imperialism."
"Dependency theory has lost its relevance in the age of globalisation." Discuss.
"Explain Wallerstein's world-system theory. How useful is it for understanding North-South relations?"

Structure: core assumptions (class, capitalism, structure). Then the three families: classical (Lenin, Hobson), dependency (Prebisch, Frank, Amin, Cardoso) and world-system (Wallerstein), plus Gramsci and Cox. Give the core-periphery diagram. Then critique: East Asia, reductionism. Close with India: Naoroji's drain, NIEO, India as semi-periphery.

Write the thinkers with titles and years. This is where marks are won.

quiz.q: Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism was written in:
Which thinker wrote Imperialism: A Study (1902) on underconsumption?
quiz.w: Hobson, a British liberal, was the main source for Lenin.

o: A peaceful joint rule by great powers
quiz.w: Kautsky saw cartelised, cooperative capitalism among great powers.

quiz.q: Raul Prebisch and Hans Singer argued that:
o: Colonies should export more raw materials
Free trade benefits primary exporters most
Terms of trade deteriorate for primary exporters
quiz.w: The Prebisch-Singer thesis says primary prices fall relative to manufactures.
Dependent countries can grow, but on terms set by the core.

o: Is exploited by the core and exploits the periphery
Is a colony of the periphery
quiz.w: It acts as a buffer and stabilises the system.
Cox said theory is always for someone and for some purpose.

quiz.q: Which fact is the strongest empirical challenge to dependency theory?
o: Rise of South Korea and Taiwan
quiz.w: East Asian tigers grew rapidly while integrated into the world market.

quiz.q: Dadabhai Naoroji's Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) is associated with:
quiz.w: Naoroji's drain theory argued Britain extracted resources from India.
